rtk.name: RTK / RAS / MAPK
rtk.mech: Growth-factor receptors dimerise and trans-autophosphorylate. SHP2, GRB2 and SOS load GTP onto RAS; RAF dimers phosphorylate MEK, MEK phosphorylates ERK, and ERK switches on the immediate-early programme (AP-1, ETS, MYC stabilisation, cyclin D1) that carries a cell past the restriction point.
rtk.lesion: Hotspot mutations lock RAS in the GTP-bound state (KRAS G12/G13/Q61) or let BRAF signal as a monomer (V600E). EGFR, ERBB2, MET and FGFR are amplified; ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK and FGFR2/3 form kinase fusions; NF1, the RasGAP, is lost. RTK, RAS and RAF lesions are strongly mutually exclusive: one hit per tumour usually saturates the pathway [1].
rtk.where: The most frequently altered pathway: a median 46% of tumours across 33 types, and 95% of melanoma, 84% of thyroid, 78% of pancreatic and 74% of lung adenocarcinoma [1].
rtk.vuln: The founding case of oncogene addiction [25]. Inhibitors of EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK and BRAF+MEK; KRAS G12C inhibitors (sotorasib, adagrasib) with G12D and RAS(ON) inhibitors in trials; HER2 antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates. Relief of ERK-dependent negative feedback limits single agents.
steps: A ligand activates its receptor

EGF, HGF, FGF or PDGF binds the extracellular domain. The receptors dimerise and their kinase domains phosphorylate each other's C-terminal tyrosines. Those phosphotyrosines become docking sites for SH2-domain adaptors (GRB2, SHC) and for the phosphatase SHP2.
RAS is loaded with GTP

GRB2 brings the exchange factor SOS to the membrane, where it swaps GDP for GTP on RAS. RAS is a binary switch: bound to GTP it is on. GTPase-activating proteins such as NF1 switch it off by speeding up its weak intrinsic GTPase.
RAF kinases dimerise

RAS-GTP recruits ARAF, BRAF and CRAF to the membrane and promotes RAF dimers. BRAF V600E skips this step and signals as a monomer. That is why first-generation BRAF inhibitors work on V600E tumours but can paradoxically activate wild-type RAF dimers in RAS-mutant cells.
MEK and ERK relay the signal
RAF phosphorylates MEK1/2, which phosphorylates ERK1/2 on its activation loop. ERK then phosphorylates hundreds of substrates, including ETS transcription factors, RSK and MYC (serine 62).
The nucleus commits to division

ERK induces FOS, cyclin D1 and MYC, which carry the cell through the G1 restriction point. ERK also induces DUSP and SPRY feedback inhibitors. When a drug blocks the pathway this feedback is released, so signalling partly recovers, which is the basis of adaptive resistance.
How cancer breaks it

Mutations lock the switch on. KRAS G12, G13 and Q61 impair GAP-driven GTP hydrolysis; EGFR kinase mutations and ERBB2 amplification make receptors constitutively active; the EML4–ALK fusion forces the kinase to dimerise. Dramatic responses to gefitinib in EGFR-mutant lung cancer showed that tumours depend on these lesions.
evidence: HER2/neu amplification predicts relapse and shorter survival in breast cancer, the first link between an amplified oncogene and outcome.
BRAF is mutated in about two thirds of melanomas, mostly at V600.
Activating EGFR kinase-domain mutations explain which lung cancers respond to gefitinib.
EML4–ALK is a transforming fusion kinase in non-small-cell lung cancer.
Covalent compounds that bind a pocket under switch II trap KRAS G12C in its inactive GDP state, ending the idea that RAS cannot be drugged.
AMG 510 (sotorasib) regresses KRAS G12C tumours and boosts anti-tumour immunity; in CodeBreaK 100, 37% of patients with KRAS G12C lung cancer responded.
therapies: EGFR exon-20 insertion and common-mutation NSCLC
HER2-positive and HER2-low breast; HER2-mutant NSCLC
RET-fusion NSCLC and thyroid; RET-mutant medullary thyroid
Melanoma, NSCLC, anaplastic thyroid; BRAF V600E tissue-agnostic
KRAS G12C NSCLC; colorectal with anti-EGFR
KRAS-mutant pancreatic, lung and colorectal cancer

cc.name: Cell cycle / RB axis
cc.mech: Mitogen-induced cyclin D–CDK4/6, then cyclin E–CDK2, phosphorylate RB and release E2F to transcribe S-phase genes. INK4 proteins (p16, p15) and CIP/KIP proteins (p21, p27) restrain the kinases. This restriction point is the decision every tumour has to take over.
cc.lesion: Homozygous deletion of CDKN2A at 9p21, among the most frequent focal deletions in cancer [11]; amplification of CCND1, CDK4/6 and CCNE1; loss of RB1, the original two-hit suppressor [18]. Lesions are mutually exclusive along the axis. Because CDKN2A also encodes ARF, a single 9p21 deletion disables both RB and p53 control, and it is mutually exclusive with TP53 mutation [1].
cc.where: Common in nearly every carcinoma, glioblastoma and melanoma; rarely altered in uveal melanoma, thymoma, testicular cancer and AML [1].
cc.vuln: CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) need intact RB. RB1 loss and CCNE1 amplification cause resistance. CDK2, WEE1 and PKMYT1 inhibitors target CCNE1-amplified, replication-stressed tumours.
steps: Mitogens make cyclin D
RAS–ERK and PI3K–mTOR signalling raise cyclin D transcription and translation. Cyclin D assembles with CDK4 or CDK6.
RB is phosphorylated
Cyclin D–CDK4/6 begins phosphorylating RB; cyclin E–CDK2 then hyperphosphorylates it and RB releases the E2F transcription factors.
E2F passes the restriction point
E2F transcribes cyclin E, cyclin A and DNA-replication genes. Cyclin E feeds back on RB, so commitment becomes irreversible and the cell no longer needs mitogens to finish the cycle.
Brakes hold the kinases
p16INK4a binds and inhibits CDK4/6 specifically. p21 and p27 inhibit CDK2. TGFβ induces p15 and p21, and p53 induces p21.
Oncogenic stress triggers senescence
Strong oncogene signalling induces p16 and ARF, arresting the cell permanently. Progression to cancer requires disabling this brake.
How cancer breaks it
CDKN2A is deleted, CCND1 and CDK4 are amplified, RB1 is lost or CCNE1 is amplified, mostly one per tumour. Retinoblastoma gave the first model: two hits inactivate both RB1 alleles.
evidence: Retinoblastoma incidence fits a two-hit model: one hit inherited or somatic, the second somatic.
p16 is a specific inhibitor of cyclin D–CDK4.
RB is defined as the gatekeeper of the restriction point controlled by G1 CDKs.
PALOMA-2: palbociclib plus letrozole extends progression-free survival from 14.5 to 24.8 months in ER+ breast cancer.
therapies: HR+/HER2− breast cancer, including high-risk adjuvant
Protects bone marrow during SCLC chemotherapy

p53.name: p53 axis
p53.mech: p53 integrates DNA damage, oncogenic stress (through ARF), hypoxia and nucleotide imbalance into arrest (p21), apoptosis (PUMA, NOXA, BAX) or senescence. MDM2 ubiquitinates p53 and MDM4 masks its transactivation domain; p53 induces MDM2, closing a negative feedback loop. ATM/ATR and CHK2/CHK1 stabilise p53 after damage.
p53.lesion: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer. Missense hotspots in the DNA-binding domain (R175, R248, R273) act as dominant negatives and are usually followed by loss of the wild-type allele. Where TP53 is intact, MDM2 or MDM4 amplification, or CDKN2A/ARF deletion, disables the pathway instead. The p53 and cell-cycle pathways are co-altered more often than any other pair [1].
p53.where: About 96% of high-grade serous ovarian cancer and about 90% of lung squamous carcinoma; most chromosomally unstable carcinomas. Wild-type in MDM2-amplified liposarcoma.
p53.vuln: MDM2 antagonists for TP53-wild-type, MDM2-amplified tumours (in dedifferentiated liposarcoma 78% co-amplify MDM2 and CDK4 [1]); small-molecule reactivators of the Y220C mutant; WEE1 and ATR inhibitors exploit the lost G1 checkpoint.
steps: p53 is kept low at rest
MDM2 ubiquitinates p53 for degradation and MDM4 blocks its transactivation domain. MDM2 was found amplified in sarcomas, where it binds p53 and silences it.
Stress stabilises p53

DNA breaks activate ATM and CHK2; replication stress activates ATR and CHK1. Phosphorylation of the p53 N-terminus blocks MDM2 binding. Oncogene signalling induces ARF through E2F, and ARF sequesters MDM2.
A tetramer binds DNA
p53 binds its response elements as a tetramer. Missense mutants in the DNA-binding domain cannot bind DNA and poison wild-type subunits in mixed tetramers (dominant-negative effect).
The cell chooses an outcome
p53 targets include p21 (arrest), PUMA, NOXA and BAX (apoptosis), senescence genes, and metabolic and ferroptosis regulators. Which outcome occurs depends on tissue and stress.
Negative feedback
p53 induces MDM2, which degrades p53, so p53 levels pulse after damage rather than rising steadily.
How cancer breaks it
TP53 mutation with loss of the second allele, or, in TP53-wild-type tumours, MDM2/MDM4 amplification or CDKN2A deletion. These routes are mutually exclusive.
evidence: MDM2 is amplified in human sarcomas and binds p53.
The MDM2 protein forms a complex with p53 and inhibits p53-driven transcription.
Nutlins, small molecules that fill the p53-binding pocket of MDM2, activate p53 in tumours in vivo.
p53 output depends on cell type and stress; tumour suppression may rest on less-studied programmes beyond arrest and apoptosis.
therapies: TP53-wild-type, MDM2-amplified tumours such as dedifferentiated liposarcoma
TP53-mutant MDS (phase 3 missed its primary endpoint)
TP53-mutant tumours that rely on the G2 checkpoint

pi3k.name: PI3K / AKT / mTOR
pi3k.mech: Class IA PI3K (p110α with p85) phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 and recruits AKT and PDK1. AKT inhibits TSC1/2, activating mTORC1 and anabolic translation, and inactivates FOXO and GSK3. PTEN removes PIP3 and is the main brake. LKB1–AMPK holds mTORC1 back under energy stress.
pi3k.lesion: PIK3CA helical (E542K, E545K) and kinase-domain (H1047R) hotspots; PIK3R1 in-frame deletions that release p110; PTEN deletion, mutation or silencing; AKT1 E17K; TSC1/2 and MTOR mutations; STK11 loss. RTK activation is mutually exclusive with PI3K lesions, while PI3K and NRF2 lesions co-occur more strongly than any other pathway pair [1].
pi3k.where: Non-hypermutated endometrial cancer (86–95%), EBV-positive gastric (80%), lung squamous (68%) [1]; also breast, head and neck, cervical, glioblastoma, prostate.
pi3k.vuln: Alpelisib and inavolisib (PIK3CA), capivasertib (AKT), everolimus (mTORC1). Insulin feedback and the p110β dependence of PTEN-null cells complicate targeting.
steps: PI3K is recruited
Phosphotyrosines on activated receptors or adaptors (and RAS-GTP) bind the SH2 domains of p85. This relieves p85's inhibition of the catalytic subunit p110α and brings it to the membrane.
PIP3 is made
p110α phosphorylates PIP2 at the 3′ position of the inositol ring to make PIP3. PTEN is the lipid phosphatase that reverses the reaction and so sets the level of signalling.
AKT is activated
PIP3 recruits AKT and PDK1 through their PH domains. PDK1 phosphorylates AKT at T308 and mTORC2 at S473, switching it fully on.
AKT phosphorylates its targets

AKT inhibits TSC2 (activating RHEB and mTORC1), excludes FOXO transcription factors from the nucleus, inactivates GSK3, inhibits the pro-apoptotic BAD and activates MDM2. The cell grows, survives and stops repairing its brakes.
mTORC1 drives anabolism
mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K and 4E-BP1, switching on cap-dependent translation and lipid and nucleotide synthesis. LKB1–AMPK (energy) and amino-acid sensing gate this step.
Feedback limits the pathway
S6K phosphorylates IRS1 and shuts down upstream signalling. Drugs release this brake. PI3Kα inhibition also raises blood glucose and insulin, which re-activates the pathway in the tumour.
How cancer breaks it
PIK3CA mutations cluster in the helical and kinase domains across many cancers. PTEN is deleted, mutated or silenced, and PI3K lesions are mutually exclusive with RTK activation within a tumour.
evidence: PTEN is identified at 10q23 and found mutated in brain, breast and prostate cancer.
PIK3CA is mutated at high frequency across human cancers, mostly in the helical and kinase domains.
SOLAR-1: alpelisib plus fulvestrant roughly doubles progression-free survival (11.0 vs 5.7 months) in PIK3CA-mutant HR+ breast cancer.
CAPItello-291: capivasertib plus fulvestrant improves progression-free survival (7.2 vs 3.6 months) in HR+ breast cancer.
therapies: PIK3CA-mutant HR+ breast cancer, with palbociclib and fulvestrant
HR+ breast, renal cell, neuroendocrine tumours, TSC

myc.name: MYC network
myc.mech: MYC–MAX heterodimers bind E-boxes and amplify transcription of genes for ribosome biogenesis, nucleotide and glutamine metabolism and cell-cycle entry. MXD, MNT and MGA, also partnered with MAX, oppose it. MYC is short-lived: ERK phosphorylates S62, GSK3 phosphorylates T58, and the resulting degron is read by FBXW7.
myc.lesion: Focal and arm-level 8q24 gain, among the most common amplifications in cancer [11]; immunoglobulin translocations in Burkitt lymphoma; MYCN amplification in neuroblastoma and MYCL in small-cell lung cancer; loss of the MGA/MAX antagonists; FBXW7 loss, which stabilises MYC.
myc.where: Most common in tumours with chromosome 8 gain: breast, ovarian, squamous carcinomas, prostate [1].
myc.vuln: No approved direct inhibitor. Indirect routes include BET, CDK7 and CDK9 inhibitors, synthetic-lethal partners, and the OMO-103 mini-protein in early trials.
steps: Many pathways converge on MYC
ERK, WNT–TCF and NOTCH–RBPJ all drive MYC transcription. MYC mRNA and protein are very short-lived, so MYC levels track signalling closely.
MYC pairs with MAX
MYC is a basic helix-loop-helix leucine-zipper protein. It must dimerise with MAX to bind E-box DNA (CACGTG).
MYC amplifies transcription
At high levels MYC invades enhancers and amplifies already-active genes, especially those for ribosome biogenesis, nucleotide synthesis and glutamine metabolism.
Antagonists compete for MAX
MXD, MNT and MGA also dimerise with MAX and repress the same sites, so losing them raises MYC output.
MYC is degraded
ERK phosphorylates S62, then GSK3 phosphorylates T58, creating a degron recognised by FBXW7. T58 mutations in Burkitt lymphoma and FBXW7 loss both stabilise MYC.
How cancer breaks it
8q24 gain and focal amplification, immunoglobulin translocations, MYCN and MYCL amplification. MYC needs anti-apoptotic partners to transform: BCL2 cooperates with MYC to immortalise pre-B cells.
evidence: BCL2 promotes survival rather than proliferation and cooperates with MYC in transformation.
Review of MYC as a global amplifier of growth programmes and a metabolic regulator.
MYC is among the most frequent focal amplifications across cancer types.

wnt.name: WNT / β-catenin
wnt.mech: Without ligand, the destruction complex (AXIN, APC, CK1, GSK3) phosphorylates β-catenin for βTrCP-mediated degradation. WNT bound to FZD and LRP6 sequesters AXIN, so β-catenin accumulates and drives TCF/LEF targets (MYC, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5). RNF43 and ZNRF3 clear FZD from the cell surface and are opposed by R-spondin and LGR5.
wnt.lesion: Truncating APC mutations, the initiating gatekeeper in about 80% of colorectal cancer [6]; CTNNB1 exon-3 degron mutations (liver, endometrium); AXIN1 loss (liver); RNF43 loss (MSI colorectal, gastric); RSPO2/3 fusions.
wnt.where: The most variable pathway across cancer types [1]: dominant in colorectal, hepatocellular and endometrioid cancers, nearly absent elsewhere.
wnt.vuln: Porcupine inhibitors work only for ligand-dependent RNF43- or RSPO-driven tumours; APC and CTNNB1 mutants signal without ligand. β-catenin activation correlates with T-cell exclusion [14].
steps: The off state degrades β-catenin
The destruction complex (AXIN, APC, CK1α, GSK3) phosphorylates β-catenin at S45, then S33, S37 and T41. βTrCP ubiquitinates it for degradation.
WNT turns the pathway on
WNT binds Frizzled and LRP5/6. Dishevelled polymerises, phosphorylated LRP6 sequesters AXIN and inhibits GSK3, and β-catenin stops being degraded.
β-catenin enters the nucleus
β-catenin binds TCF/LEF, displaces Groucho co-repressors and transcribes MYC, CCND1, AXIN2 and LGR5.
Surface receptors are tuned
RNF43 and ZNRF3 ubiquitinate Frizzled and remove it. R-spondin with LGR4/5 clears RNF43/ZNRF3, amplifying WNT signals in stem cells.
How cancer breaks it
APC loss constitutively activates β-catenin–TCF in colon cancer. Tumours with wild-type APC carry CTNNB1 mutations that remove the phosphodegron.
evidence: MMTV proviruses integrate repeatedly at one locus (int-1, later Wnt1) in mouse mammary tumours.
APC−/− colon cancer cells show constitutive β-catenin–TCF transcription.
Colon cancers and melanomas with wild-type APC carry activating β-catenin mutations.
Review of WNT signalling and therapeutic modalities.
therapies: No approved WNT-pathway drug for cancer

notch.name: NOTCH
notch.mech: DLL or JAG ligand binding triggers ADAM10 and γ-secretase cleavage. The NOTCH intracellular domain (NICD) enters the nucleus, binds RBPJ and MAML, and drives HES/HEY and, in T cells, MYC. FBXW7 ends the signal by degrading NICD.
notch.lesion: The sign depends on tissue. Oncogenic: activating NOTCH1 HD and PEST mutations in T-ALL and CLL. Suppressive: truncating NOTCH1–3 mutations in squamous carcinomas of head and neck, lung, skin and oesophagus, where Notch drives squamous differentiation. FBXW7 loss stabilises NICD, MYC, cyclin E and MCL1 at once.
notch.where: Head and neck and other squamous cancers, T-ALL, oligodendroglioma.
notch.vuln: γ-secretase inhibitors (nirogacestat, approved for desmoid tumours) carry gut toxicity, and inhibition is contraindicated where Notch acts as a suppressor.
steps: Ligand meets receptor
DLL or JAG on a neighbouring cell binds NOTCH. Endocytosis of the ligand pulls on the receptor and exposes its S2 cleavage site.
Two cuts release NICD
ADAM10 cuts at S2, then γ-secretase cuts within the membrane (S3), releasing the NOTCH intracellular domain (NICD).
A nuclear complex forms
NICD binds RBPJ and recruits MAML, turning RBPJ from a repressor into an activator. Targets include HES1, HEY genes and, in T cells, MYC.
The signal is terminated
The PEST domain of NICD is phosphorylated and recognised by FBXW7, which targets it for degradation.
Oncogenic in T cells
More than half of T-ALLs carry activating NOTCH1 mutations in the heterodimerisation (HD) domain, which allows cleavage without ligand, or in the PEST domain, which blocks degradation.
Suppressive in squamous epithelia
Inactivating NOTCH1 mutations occur in head and neck squamous carcinoma, where Notch drives differentiation.
evidence: Activating NOTCH1 mutations are found in more than 50% of human T-ALL.
Exome sequencing finds inactivating NOTCH1 mutations in head and neck squamous carcinoma.
DeFi trial: the γ-secretase inhibitor nirogacestat cuts progression risk by 71% in desmoid tumours.
therapies: DLL3 × CD3 bispecific (DLL3 as surface antigen, not pathway blockade)

hippo.name: Hippo / YAP–TAZ
hippo.mech: Cell density, polarity and mechanical cues activate MST1/2–SAV1 and MAP4K kinases, which phosphorylate LATS1/2. LATS phosphorylates YAP and TAZ, holding them in the cytoplasm. Unphosphorylated YAP/TAZ bind TEAD and drive proliferation and survival genes (CTGF, CYR61, AXL).
hippo.lesion: NF2 loss (mesothelioma, schwannoma), LATS1/2 and SAV1 loss, FAT1 truncation (head and neck, lung squamous), YAP1 and WWTR1 (TAZ) fusions, YAP1 amplification. Hippo lesions often co-occur in the same tumour, which suggests they cooperate to activate YAP [1].
hippo.where: Mesothelioma, head and neck, lung squamous, uveal melanoma (through GNAQ/11), renal.
hippo.vuln: TEAD palmitoylation inhibitors are in early trials. YAP/TAZ also mediate resistance to RAS–MAPK inhibitors.
steps: Cells sense their surroundings
Cell–cell contact, polarity complexes, NF2/Merlin, FAT cadherins and mechanical tension on actin all feed into the Hippo kinases.
A kinase cascade fires
MST1/2 (with SAV1) and MAP4K kinases phosphorylate LATS1/2, which work together with MOB1.
YAP and TAZ are inactivated
LATS phosphorylates YAP at S127, creating a 14-3-3 binding site that holds YAP in the cytoplasm. Contact inhibition of growth depends on this step.
Nuclear YAP/TAZ drive growth
When Hippo is off, YAP/TAZ enter the nucleus, bind TEAD and drive CTGF, CYR61 and AXL, often together with AP-1 at enhancers.
How cancer breaks it
NF2 and LATS loss, FAT1 truncation, YAP1 and TAZ fusions, and GNAQ/GNA11 mutations in uveal melanoma that activate YAP through RHO. Hippo lesions tend to co-occur within a tumour.
evidence: The Hippo pathway inactivates YAP, and this mediates contact inhibition and organ-size control.
Hippo pathway lesions often co-occur within a tumour, suggesting they cooperate.
therapies: NF2-mutant mesothelioma and other YAP-driven tumours

tgfb.name: TGFβ / SMAD
tgfb.mech: TGFβ binds TGFBR2, which phosphorylates TGFBR1. SMAD2/3 are phosphorylated, partner with SMAD4, induce p15 and p21 and repress MYC, a cytostatic programme in epithelia. In advanced tumours the same ligand promotes EMT, invasion, fibrosis and immune exclusion.
tgfb.lesion: SMAD4 deletion or mutation (pancreas, colorectal); TGFBR2 and ACVR2A frameshifts at poly-A tracts in MSI tumours; SMAD2/3 mutations. Late tumours keep the ligand while losing the cytostatic response.
tgfb.where: Highest in pancreatic and gastrointestinal cancers; renal and brain cancers have almost none [1].
tgfb.vuln: TGFβ traps and ALK5 inhibitors have given mixed results. Stromal TGFβ defines the TGF-β-dominant immune subtype and excludes T cells [14].
steps: The ligand is released
TGFβ is secreted in a latent complex. Integrins and proteases release the active ligand.
Receptors phosphorylate each other
TGFβ binds TGFBR2, which phosphorylates the GS domain of TGFBR1 (ALK5).
SMADs carry the signal
ALK5 phosphorylates the C-terminus of SMAD2/3. They bind SMAD4 and the complex enters the nucleus.
Epithelial cells stop dividing
SMAD complexes induce CDKN2B (p15) and CDKN1A (p21) and repress MYC and ID genes.
The response switches
Advanced tumours lose the cytostatic arm but keep the ligand, which now drives EMT, invasion, fibrosis and immune suppression.
How cancer breaks it
TGFBR2 is inactivated by frameshifts at a poly-A tract in MSI colon cancer, and SMAD4 (DPC4) is deleted at 18q21 in pancreatic cancer.
evidence: TGFBR2 is inactivated in colon cancers with microsatellite instability.
DPC4 (SMAD4) is identified as a tumour suppressor at 18q21.1, homozygously deleted in pancreatic cancer.
TGFβ switches from suppressor to promoter during tumour progression.
A TGF-β-dominant immune subtype has poor prognosis across tumour types.
therapies: Anaemia in lower-risk MDS (supportive, not antitumour)

nrf2.name: KEAP1 / NRF2 oxidative stress
nrf2.mech: KEAP1 is the substrate adaptor of a CUL3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades NRF2 at rest. Oxidants and electrophiles modify KEAP1 cysteines; NRF2 then accumulates and induces antioxidant, NADPH-generating and drug-efflux genes.
nrf2.lesion: KEAP1 loss-of-function and NFE2L2 gain-of-function mutations in the DLG/ETGE KEAP1-binding motifs, nearly mutually exclusive; CUL3 loss; NFE2L2 amplification. NRF2 lesions co-occur with PI3K activation [1], and in lung adenocarcinoma KEAP1 loss co-occurs with STK11 loss.
nrf2.where: The lowest overall frequency (4%), but 25% of lung squamous and 23% of oesophageal squamous carcinoma [1].
nrf2.vuln: No approved direct drug; glutaminase and other metabolic dependencies are under test. KEAP1/STK11 co-mutation predicts poor response to immunotherapy.
steps: NRF2 is degraded at rest
A KEAP1 dimer grips the Neh2 domain of NRF2 at its DLG and ETGE motifs, and CUL3 ubiquitinates it.
KEAP1 senses stress
Electrophiles and oxidants modify KEAP1 cysteines (C151, C273, C288). KEAP1 can no longer present NRF2 for ubiquitination, so newly made NRF2 accumulates.
NRF2 switches on defences
NRF2 with small MAF proteins binds antioxidant response elements and induces NQO1, HMOX1, glutathione-synthesis genes, thioredoxin reductase, G6PD and drug-efflux pumps.
Metabolism is rewired
Higher NADPH and glutathione protect against oxidative stress and chemotherapy, but make cells dependent on glutamine and cystine.
How cancer breaks it
KEAP1 mutations disrupt the KEAP1–NRF2 interaction in lung cancer, and NFE2L2 motif mutations do the same in squamous cancers.
evidence: KEAP1 represses NRF2 by binding its N-terminal Neh2 domain.
KEAP1 mutations disrupt KEAP1–NRF2 binding in non-small-cell lung cancer.
NRF2 and PI3K pathway lesions co-occur more strongly than any other pathway pair.

ddr.name: DNA damage response & repair

fr.note: MMR, HR and POLE defects; frequency varies by tissue

ddr.mech: These are the caretaker networks: homologous recombination (BRCA1–PALB2–BRCA2–RAD51) for double-strand breaks and stalled forks; mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); polymerase-ε proofreading (POLE); and ATM/ATR checkpoint signalling. Each defect raises the mutation rate and leaves its own mutational signature [8].
ddr.lesion: Biallelic BRCA1/2 loss, germline or somatic, gives homologous-recombination deficiency (signature SBS3 and microhomology deletions). MLH1 promoter hypermethylation causes MSI; POLE exonuclease hotspots cause ultramutation above 100 mutations/Mb. Mutations with loss of heterozygosity affect over a third of DDR genes [13].
ddr.where: HR loss in ovarian (most common), breast, prostate and pancreatic cancer; MMR and POLE loss in colorectal, endometrial and gastric cancer.
ddr.vuln: PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality with HR loss [23]. Immune checkpoint blockade has a tissue-agnostic approval for MSI-H/dMMR tumours; more than 300 MSI tumours in TCGA show high PD-1/PD-L1 [2]. ATR, WEE1 and POLQ inhibitors are in trials.
steps: Damage is detected
The MRN complex senses double-strand breaks and activates ATM. RPA-coated single-stranded DNA at stalled forks activates ATR.
Checkpoints halt the cycle
CHK2 and CHK1 inhibit CDC25 phosphatases and stabilise p53, giving time for repair.
The cell chooses a repair route
53BP1 favours error-prone end joining. BRCA1 promotes end resection; PALB2 bridges BRCA1 to BRCA2, which loads RAD51 for homology search and accurate repair.
Mismatches are corrected
MutSα (MSH2–MSH6) recognises replication errors and MutLα (MLH1–PMS2) nicks the new strand. Loss causes microsatellite instability and a high neoantigen load.
Polymerase proofreading
The exonuclease domain of polymerase ε removes misincorporated bases. POLE hotspot mutations remove proofreading and cause ultramutation.
Synthetic lethality
PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 on DNA. HR-deficient cells cannot repair the resulting replication-associated breaks and die, while normal cells survive.
evidence: BRCA1/2-deficient cells are about a thousand-fold more sensitive to PARP inhibition than normal cells.
PD-1 blockade produces responses in mismatch-repair-deficient colorectal cancer.
MMR deficiency predicts response to PD-1 blockade across 12 tumour types.
OlympiAD: olaparib improves progression-free survival in germline BRCA-mutant metastatic breast cancer.
SOLO-1: maintenance olaparib lowers the risk of progression or death by 70% in newly diagnosed BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer.
therapies: BRCA-mutant ovarian, breast, pancreatic; HRR-mutant prostate
Germline BRCA breast; HRR-mutant prostate with enzalutamide

chrom.name: Chromatin & epigenetic regulators
chrom.mech: SWI/SNF (BAF/PBAF) remodellers open enhancers and oppose Polycomb (PRC2/EZH2) silencing. KMT2C/D with KDM6A mark enhancers; CREBBP/EP300 acetylate histones and p53; SETD2 writes H3K36me3; DNMT3A and TET2 balance DNA methylation; BAP1 removes H2AK119 ubiquitin.
chrom.lesion: Mostly truncating losses spread over many genes. mSWI/SNF subunits are mutated in 19.6% of human tumours [16]: ARID1A (ovarian clear-cell, endometrial, gastric), PBRM1 (renal), SMARCA4 (lung, SCCOHT), SMARCB1 (rhabdoid). EZH2 Y641 gain of function in lymphoma; DNMT3A and TET2 in clonal haematopoiesis and AML. Hanahan now lists non-mutational epigenetic reprogramming as an enabling characteristic [5].
chrom.where: Present in almost every tumour type. Clear-cell renal (PBRM1, SETD2, BAP1 on 3p), bladder (KDM6A, KMT2D), lymphoma (CREBBP, KMT2D, EZH2).
chrom.vuln: Tazemetostat (EZH2) for SMARCB1-deficient sarcoma and follicular lymphoma; paralog synthetic lethality (ARID1A–ARID1B, SMARCA4–SMARCA2) with SMARCA2 degraders in trials; hypomethylating agents in myeloid disease.
steps: Nucleosomes are moved
SWI/SNF (BAF and PBAF) uses ATP, through SMARCA4 or SMARCA2, to slide or evict nucleosomes at enhancers and promoters. ARID1A and PBRM1 target the complexes to DNA.
SWI/SNF opposes Polycomb
SWI/SNF evicts PRC2. When SWI/SNF is lost, EZH2-catalysed H3K27me3 spreads, so SMARCB1- and ARID1A-deficient cells become dependent on EZH2.
Enhancers are written
KMT2C/D place H3K4me1, KDM6A removes the repressive H3K27me3 mark, and CREBBP/EP300 add H3K27ac to activate enhancers.
DNA methylation is balanced
DNMT3A writes new DNA methylation and TET2 oxidises it for removal. 2-hydroxyglutarate made by mutant IDH inhibits TET enzymes.
How cancer breaks it
Truncating SMARCB1 mutations cause rhabdoid tumours, ARID1A mutations ovarian clear-cell carcinoma, PBRM1 mutations renal carcinoma. Overall about a fifth of tumours mutate SWI/SNF.
evidence: Truncating hSNF5/INI1 (SMARCB1) mutations cause aggressive paediatric rhabdoid tumours.
ARID1A is mutated in endometriosis-associated ovarian carcinomas.
PBRM1 is frequently mutated in clear-cell renal carcinoma.
mSWI/SNF subunits are mutated in 19.6% of human tumours.
ARID1A-mutant cancers depend on EZH2 methyltransferase activity (synthetic lethality).
therapies: INI1-deficient epithelioid sarcoma; relapsed follicular lymphoma

telo.name: Telomere maintenance

fr.note: TERT promoter: most frequent non-coding driver

telo.mech: Telomeres shorten with each division and critically short telomeres trigger crisis. Cancers either reactivate telomerase (TERT) or use ALT, a recombination-based mechanism normally suppressed by the ATRX–DAXX histone H3.3 chaperone.
telo.lesion: TERT promoter mutations (C228T, C250T) create new ETS/GABP binding sites; they were found in melanoma [20, 21] and are the most common non-coding driver in whole genomes [7]. TERT is also amplified and rearranged, and MYC activates it. ATRX/DAXX loss gives ALT.
telo.where: TERT promoter: melanoma, glioblastoma, oligodendroglioma, bladder, hepatocellular, aggressive thyroid. ALT: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, IDH-mutant astrocytoma, sarcomas, often from tissues with low replicative activity [7].
telo.vuln: Imetelstat, a telomerase-targeting oligonucleotide, is approved in MDS. Telomerase-dependent nucleosides such as 6-thio-dG are experimental.
steps: Telomeres shorten
Conventional replication cannot fully copy chromosome ends, so telomeres lose sequence with each division. The shelterin complex caps the ends.
Crisis
Critically short telomeres trigger p53- and RB-dependent senescence. Cells without those checkpoints keep dividing until chromosome fusions and breakage cause crisis.
Telomerase extends the ends
TERT uses its RNA template TERC to add TTAGGG repeats. Telomerase activity is present in most tumours but absent from most normal somatic tissues.
Promoter mutations reactivate TERT
C228T and C250T mutations create new ETS-factor binding sites that recruit GABP and switch TERT on.
Alternative lengthening
ATRX or DAXX loss permits ALT, which maintains telomeres by recombination.
evidence: Telomerase activity is detected in most immortal cell lines and tumours but not in normal somatic tissues.
ATRX and DAXX mutations correlate with ALT in tumours.
Highly recurrent TERT promoter mutations in melanoma.
TERT promoter mutation is the most frequent non-coding driver in whole cancer genomes.

apop.name: Intrinsic apoptosis
apop.mech: BH3-only sensors (BIM, PUMA, NOXA) neutralise anti-apoptotic BCL2, BCL-XL and MCL1. This frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane, and cytochrome c drives APAF1, caspase-9 and caspase-3. The extrinsic arm runs through death receptors and caspase-8.
apop.lesion: BCL2 t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma; focal amplification of MCL1 and BCL2L1, among the most frequent in cancer [11]; loss of p53-driven PUMA/NOXA induction; CASP8 mutation in head and neck and cervical cancer; BAX frameshifts in MSI tumours.
apop.where: Lymphoid neoplasms (BCL2), breast and lung (MCL1), and functionally most TP53-mutant tumours.
apop.vuln: Venetoclax (BCL2) in CLL and AML. MCL1 inhibitors are limited by cardiac toxicity. BH3 profiling measures how close a tumour is to the apoptotic threshold.
steps: Sensors detect damage
BH3-only proteins are induced by p53 (PUMA, NOXA), released from the cytoskeleton (BIM, BMF) or cleaved by caspase-8 (BID).
Guardians hold the line
BCL2, BCL-XL and MCL1 bind and neutralise BH3-only proteins and BAX/BAK.
The mitochondria are permeabilised
Freed BAX and BAK oligomerise in the mitochondrial outer membrane. Cytochrome c escapes, forms the apoptosome with APAF1 and activates caspase-9, then caspase-3 and caspase-7.
Survival as an oncogenic function
BCL2 promotes survival rather than proliferation, and it cooperates with MYC to transform cells.
BH3 mimetics
Venetoclax mimics BH3 proteins and selectively inhibits BCL2. Because it spares BCL-XL, it avoids the platelet loss seen with earlier compounds.
evidence: BCL2 promotes haemopoietic cell survival and cooperates with c-myc.
ABT-199 (venetoclax) is selective for BCL2 and spares platelets.
Venetoclax gives a 79% response rate in relapsed CLL.
VIALE-A: azacitidine plus venetoclax extends median survival from 9.6 to 14.7 months in unfit AML.
therapies: CLL; AML with azacitidine or low-dose cytarabine

immune.name: Antigen presentation & immune evasion
immune.mech: HLA class I molecules, which need β2-microglobulin, present neoantigens to CD8 T cells. IFN-γ signals through IFNGR, JAK1/2, STAT1 and IRF1 to raise HLA and PD-L1. Tumours escape by losing presentation, losing interferon sensing or engaging checkpoints.
immune.lesion: Allele-specific HLA loss of heterozygosity in 40% of NSCLC [17]; B2M truncation (MSI colorectal, melanoma resistance); JAK1/2 loss (acquired anti-PD-1 resistance); 9p24 CD274/PDCD1LG2 amplification (Hodgkin lymphoma). Oncogenic pathways (WNT/β-catenin, PTEN loss) also exclude T cells.
immune.where: Six immune subtypes cut across all 33 TCGA cancer types [14]. Mutation load, MSI, APOBEC activity and HLA status shape them.
immune.vuln: PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4 and LAG-3 blockade. Responses track neoantigen load and are undone by B2M or JAK loss.
steps: Antigens are processed
The proteasome cuts tumour proteins, TAP moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, and they are loaded onto HLA class I with β2-microglobulin.
T cells are primed
Dendritic cells present tumour antigen in lymph nodes. CTLA-4 limits co-stimulation, and blocking it enhances anti-tumour immunity.
Effector T cells attack
CD8 T cells secrete IFN-γ. In the tumour, IFNGR–JAK1/2–STAT1–IRF1 signalling raises HLA and PD-L1 (adaptive resistance).
Checkpoints brake the attack
PD-1 on T cells binds PD-L1 and dampens killing. Response to PD-1 blockade tracks tumour mutation burden.
How cancer escapes
Loss of JAK1/2 or B2M causes acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, and allele-specific HLA loss removes neoantigen presentation.
evidence: CTLA-4 blockade enhances anti-tumour immunity in mice.
Ipilimumab improves overall survival in metastatic melanoma.
Mutation burden determines sensitivity to PD-1 blockade in NSCLC.
JAK1/2 and B2M mutations underlie acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade in melanoma.
HLA loss of heterozygosity occurs in 40% of NSCLC.
therapies: Many solid tumours and Hodgkin lymphoma
NSCLC, SCLC, urothelial, Merkel cell, HCC

metab.name: Metabolic & hypoxia sensing

fr.note: VHL ≈90% of clear-cell renal; IDH in glioma and AML

metab.mech: The VHL ubiquitin ligase degrades prolyl-hydroxylated HIF-α in normal oxygen. Without VHL, HIF-2α is stable and drives VEGF, glycolysis and EPO programmes. Mutant IDH1 (R132) and IDH2 (R140, R172) gain a new activity that makes 2-hydroxyglutarate [22], which inhibits TET and Jumonji demethylases and links metabolism to chromatin.
metab.lesion: Biallelic VHL loss (3p loss plus mutation or methylation) in about 90% of clear-cell renal cancer; IDH1/2 hotspots in glioma, AML, cholangiocarcinoma and chondrosarcoma; SDH and FH loss in paraganglioma and hereditary renal cancer, accumulating succinate and fumarate.
metab.vuln: Belzutifan (HIF-2α) for VHL disease and renal cancer; ivosidenib, enasidenib and vorasidenib (mutant IDH); anti-angiogenic VEGF/VEGFR drugs.
steps: Oxygen is sensed
PHD enzymes use oxygen and α-ketoglutarate to hydroxylate prolines on HIF-α. VHL binds hydroxylated HIF-α and targets it for degradation.
Hypoxia stabilises HIF
Without oxygen, HIF-α escapes VHL, pairs with ARNT and drives VEGFA, GLUT1, LDHA and EPO.
VHL loss mimics hypoxia
VHL, the gene behind VHL disease, is inactivated in most clear-cell renal cancers, and HIF-2α becomes the driver.
Oncometabolites block demethylases

Mutant IDH1 R132, discovered by glioblastoma genomics, makes 2-hydroxyglutarate. 2-HG, succinate (SDH loss) and fumarate (FH loss) all inhibit α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases such as TET and KDM enzymes.
Energy is sensed
LKB1 activates AMPK when energy is low, and AMPK restrains mTORC1. STK11 loss removes this brake.
evidence: The VHL tumour suppressor gene is identified.
VHL targets HIF for oxygen-dependent proteolysis.
IDH1 R132 mutations are discovered in glioblastoma.
Mutant IDH1 produces 2-hydroxyglutarate.
Ivosidenib produces durable remissions in IDH1-mutant relapsed AML.
Belzutifan gives a 49% response rate in VHL-disease renal cancer.
INDIGO: vorasidenib extends progression-free survival (27.7 vs 11.1 months) in IDH-mutant low-grade glioma.
therapies: VHL-disease tumours; advanced renal cell carcinoma
Colorectal, lung, renal, glioblastoma, ovarian, HCC

splice.name: RNA splicing
splice.mech: Core spliceosome factors recognise branch points (SF3B1) and 3′ splice sites (U2AF1), and SR proteins such as SRSF2 guide exon choice.
splice.lesion: Heterozygous hotspot mutations: SF3B1 K700E (MDS with ring sideroblasts, CLL, uveal melanoma, breast), U2AF1 S34/Q157 (MDS, lung adenocarcinoma), SRSF2 P95 (CMML). They change splice-site choice without abolishing splicing, and they are mutually exclusive, which implies cells tolerate only one.
splice.vuln: Splicing modulators (SF3B1-targeted) and dependence on the remaining wild-type allele.
steps: The spliceosome assembles
U1 snRNP binds the 5′ splice site; SF1 and U2AF bind the branch point and 3′ splice site; U2 snRNP, through SF3B1, base-pairs with the branch point.
Hotspots alter, not abolish
Mutations in U2AF1, SRSF2, ZRSR2 and SF3B1 occur in myelodysplasia and are mutually exclusive.
Mis-splicing has consequences
SF3B1 K700E uses cryptic 3′ splice sites, sending transcripts such as ABCB7 to nonsense-mediated decay. This links the mutation to ring sideroblasts.
A built-in vulnerability
Mutant cells depend on the remaining wild-type allele, which makes them more sensitive to spliceosome modulators.
evidence: Frequent mutations of the splicing machinery in myelodysplasia.
therapies: Anaemia in lower-risk MDS, especially SF3B1-mutant ring-sideroblast MDS

principles: Convergence

Hundreds of driver genes (299 in the PanCancer driver census [2]; saturation analysis predicted that many more rare ones remain [10]) funnel into a small number of circuits. 89% of TCGA tumours carry a driver lesion in one of only ten pathways [1], and the average genome has four to five drivers [7]. Selection acts on pathway output, not on individual genes.
Two accelerators, two brakes

The minimal topology of most carcinomas is one activated growth-factor axis (RTK–RAS–MAPK or PI3K–mTOR) plus disabled RB and p53 checkpoints [6]. The two axes converge on MYC, cyclin D and mTORC1. The 9p21 deletion of CDKN2A shows the economy of selection: one event removes p16 (RB control) and ARF (p53 control).
Mutual exclusivity reveals the unit of selection

RTK, RAS and RAF lesions rarely co-occur in one tumour, and neither do TP53 and MDM2 lesions [1]. Once a pathway is switched, a second hit adds little or is harmful (oncogene-induced stress). Co-occurrence instead marks synergy, as with PI3K and NRF2 [1] or multiple Hippo lesions.
Tissue decides which gene

The pathway is shared but the gene is chosen by the cell of origin: KRAS in pancreas, BRAF in thyroid and melanoma, EGFR in glioblastoma, APC in colon. Molecular classification of 10,000 tumours is dominated by tissue of origin [15]. Notch is oncogenic in T cells and suppressive in squamous epithelia.
Gatekeepers and caretakers

Gatekeepers (APC, RB1, TP53, VHL) control cell number directly; Knudson's two hits [18] usually take the form of a point mutation plus loss of heterozygosity. Caretakers (BRCA1/2, MMR, POLE) raise the mutation rate and leave signatures that record a tumour's history [8, 13].
Drivers are necessary but not sufficient

Normal sun-exposed skin and oesophagus carry clones with NOTCH1, TP53 and FAT1 driver mutations at high density [24], with the same dN/dS selection seen in cancers [12]. Transformation needs combinations, tissue context and time.
Chromatin is a second genome to break

SWI/SNF alone is mutated in about one fifth of tumours [16], and enhancer regulators (KMT2C/D, KDM6A, CREBBP) rank among the most mutated genes. IDH-mutant 2-hydroxyglutarate links metabolism to methylation [22]. Hanahan's 2022 framework adds epigenetic reprogramming and plasticity [5].
Immortality and structure come from outside the exome

TERT promoter mutations are the most frequent non-coding driver [7, 20, 21]. Chromothripsis and complex structural variants, often early events, amplify or delete several drivers at once [7, 26]. Arm-level copy-number change (8q gain for MYC; 9p, 17p and 18q loss) is a major force in its own right [11].
Tumours must also hide

Immune escape is a selected phenotype: HLA LOH in 40% of NSCLC [17], B2M and JAK1/2 loss, and pathway-driven T-cell exclusion. Six immune subtypes cut across tissues [14]. MSI and POLE ultramutation make tumours visible, which is why checkpoint blockade works there [2].
Vulnerabilities follow the wiring

Oncogene addiction [25] explains why switching off a dominant node (BCR-ABL, EGFR, BRAF, KRAS G12C) can collapse a tumour. Synthetic lethality explains PARP inhibition in HR-deficient cancer [23]. 57% of tumours have at least one actionable lesion and 30% have several [1]; MSK-IMPACT confirms similar rates in metastatic disease [19]. Mutual exclusivity and feedback maps point to rational combinations.
